section.title: God Brings Down and Lifts Up
section.sectionRationale: A brief but weighty hymn of Asaph, this psalm answers the previous lament's cry for God to act with God's own declaration that He alone judges, appointing the time to bring down the proud and lift up the humble, a truth Mary would later sing in the Magnificat.
section.thesis: Because God alone holds the appointed time of judgment in His hand, exalting one and humbling another, the proud are warned not to boast while the righteous are called to thanksgiving and confident, ongoing praise.
section.frameNote: Four movements: thanksgiving for God's nearness, verse 1; God's appointed judgment and warning to the proud, verses 2 to 5; God alone exalts and judges, verses 6 to 8; ongoing praise and the final reversal, verses 9 to 10.

verses.text: For the choirmaster: To the tune of "Do Not Destroy." A Psalm of Asaph. A song. We give thanks to You, O God; we give thanks, for Your Name is near. The people declare Your wondrous works.
"When I choose a time, I will judge fairly.
When the earth and all its dwellers quake, it is I who bear up its pillars. Selah
I say to the proud, 'Do not boast,' and to the wicked, 'Do not lift up your {{qeren|horn}}.
Do not lift up your horn against heaven or speak with an outstretched neck.'"
For exaltation comes neither from east nor west, nor out of the desert,
but it is God who judges; He brings down one and exalts another.
For a {{kos|cup}} is in the hand of the LORD, full of foaming wine mixed with spices. He pours from His cup, and all the wicked of the earth drink it down to the dregs.
But I will proclaim Him forever; I will sing praise to the God of Jacob.
"All the horns of the wicked I will cut off, but the horns of the righteous will be exalted."

qeren.gloss: Horn, a symbol of strength, authority, and pride, as in an animal displaying its horns. To 'lift up the horn' pictures boastful self-exaltation; God alone decides whose horn is cut off and whose is lifted.

kos.gloss: Cup, often used in the prophets as an image of divine judgment poured out and drunk down, as here, or of blessing, depending on context; here it pictures the inescapable judgment the wicked must drink to the dregs.

basic.context: A short hymn of Asaph, likely answering the desperate plea of Psalm 74 for God to rise up, this psalm gives voice to God's own declaration that He alone appoints the time of judgment, bringing down the proud and lifting up the humble.
basic.hermeneutics: This psalm proclaims a timeless truth about God's sovereign judgment; it is not describing one isolated historical event but declaring the pattern by which God governs all human pride and humility, past, present, and future.
basic.originalLanguages: The proud are warned not to lift up their qeren, horn, a symbol of boastful strength, verses 4-5, while God's judgment is pictured as a kos, cup, of foaming wine that the wicked must drink to the dregs, verse 8.
basic.typology: The cup of God's judgment that the wicked must drink anticipates the cup of wrath Jesus drank on behalf of sinners in Gethsemane and at the cross, so that those who trust Him are spared what this psalm says the wicked cannot escape.
basic.christ: Christ prayed, 'Let this cup pass from me,' yet drank the very cup of divine judgment pictured in verse 8, Matthew 26:39, so that all who trust Him never have to drink it themselves, while His own subsequent exaltation, His horn lifted up, fulfills the psalm's promise that God exalts the righteous, Luke 1:69.
basic.god: God alone is shown to hold the timing and outcome of all judgment, unmoved by any human claim to power from any direction, bringing down the proud and lifting up the humble according to His own perfect timing.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 26:39 shows Jesus facing the cup of God's wrath this psalm pictures. Luke 1:52 has Mary sing that God 'has brought down rulers... and lifted up the humble,' directly echoing this psalm's theme. Luke 1:69 speaks of God raising up 'a horn of salvation,' the positive fulfillment of this psalm's horn imagery.
basic.oneStory: This declaration that God alone brings down the proud and lifts up the humble threads through Mary's Magnificat into the whole story of Scripture, resolved at the cross where Christ drank the cup of judgment pictured here so that all who trust Him are lifted up instead of cast down.

context.literary:
The psalm is a conversation in which the speaker keeps changing, and the changes are the structure. Verse 1 is the congregation speaking to God in the plural, 'we give thanks.' Verses 2 to 5 are a quotation, and the voice is God's own: 'When I choose a time, I will judge fairly.' Verses 6 to 8 step back into the third person and explain why, speaking about God, 'it is God who judges.' Verse 9 is a single person, 'I will proclaim Him forever,' and verse 10 returns to the divine first person with the last word. The poem is framed by thanks at the start and by God's promise at the end, and in between the human voice is only a witness to what God says.

Two Selahs mark turns, one after the claim that God holds up the pillars of the earth, verse 3, and none after the cup, which is left to hang. The centre of the psalm is the pair in verses 4 and 5, where the command 'Do not boast' and 'Do not lift up your horn' is said twice, then explained by the cup and the gift of verse 7. Horns run through the whole: the horn is lifted in verse 4, again in verse 5, and cut off or exalted in verse 10, so that the psalm begins and ends with the same image and reverses it.

The poem also plays with height and depth. 'Lift up' and 'exalt' share a family in the Hebrew, and God 'brings down one and exalts another,' verse 7. The proud reach up with an outstretched neck; the cup is poured down and must be drunk down to the dregs. The direction of the whole psalm is downward for the arrogant and upward for the righteous, and no human hand can change it.

It is a short psalm that ends on a promise, not a lament. That matters because it sits straight after a lament. Psalm 74 ends with 'the uproar of Your enemies that ascends continually,' and Psalm 75 answers with a voice that speaks in the first person from heaven.
context.historical:
The heading gives the tune 'Do Not Destroy,' the same words that stand over Psalms 57, 58 and 59. They echo the plea Moses made in the wilderness, 'do not destroy Your people, Your inheritance,' Deuteronomy 9:26. Whatever the tune was, the phrase gives the psalm an old covenant setting: a prayer in which Israel's survival is at stake and God is asked to hold back.

The psalm belongs to the Asaph collection in Book III, and the neighbouring psalms are full of enemy nations and ruined sanctuaries. In such a world the boast of a proud king was not a private vice. Assyria and Babylon spoke as though their armies, not the LORD, gave and took away kingdoms. Isaiah heard the Assyrian king say, 'By the strength of my hand I have done this,' Isaiah 10:13, and God's reply is that the axe does not boast over the one who swings it, Isaiah 10:15. The command 'Do not boast' in verse 4 belongs to the same clash between imperial pride and the God of Jacob.

The image of the horn comes from the farmyard and the battlefield. A wild ox tossing its head was the picture of unbeatable strength. Psalm 92:10 speaks of an exalted horn 'like that of a wild ox,' and Hannah's song, which this psalm resembles closely, begins with 'my horn is exalted in the LORD,' 1 Samuel 2:1. To lift up your horn is to strut in your own strength; to have it lifted for you is to be honoured by God.

The cup was a familiar picture of what a person's life was given by God. Psalm 16:5 speaks of God as 'my portion and my cup', and Psalm 11:6 says that fire and a scorching wind 'will be their portion' for the wicked. Jeremiah was told to take from God's hand 'the cup of the wine of wrath' and make the nations drink, Jeremiah 25:15-16. An Israelite hearing verse 8 would think of a banquet cup, mixed with spices to make it strong, that turns into a judgment.
context.canonical:
Set beside Psalm 74, this psalm reads as an answer. Psalm 74 lamented that the enemy had wrecked God's 'meeting places,' using the word for appointed times. Psalm 75 has God say, 'When I choose a time,' using the same word for appointment. The ruined meeting is followed by God's own appointment, and the psalmist can wait because the time belongs to God.

The song of Hannah is its closest relative. She says that the bows of the mighty are broken, that the LORD brings low and lifts up, and that 'the foundations of the earth are the LORD's,' 1 Samuel 2:4-8. Psalm 75:3 has God say he bears up the pillars of the earth. Mary's Magnificat draws on the same stream: 'He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble,' Luke 1:52, and the 'horn of salvation' of Zechariah's song, Luke 1:69, is the fulfilment of the horn imagery of verse 10.

The cup runs from Jeremiah, where the nations must drink, Jeremiah 25:15-16, to Isaiah, where Jerusalem has drunk it 'to the dregs' and God finally takes it from her hand, Isaiah 51:17 and 22. In Jesus' hands it is a cup he accepts, Matthew 26:39 and John 18:11. Revelation shows the cup finally given to those who worship the beast and to Babylon, Revelation 14:10 and 16:19.

The teaching about pride is taken up throughout the New Testament: 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble,' James 4:6, and Peter's counsel to 'humble yourselves, therefore, under God's mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you,' 1 Peter 5:6. Jesus says the same, Luke 18:14. 'In due time' is the New Testament equivalent of the psalm's 'When I choose a time.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted his congregation to stop looking for rescue in the wrong places. Verse 6 says exaltation comes from no direction of the compass, not from the east or west or the desert, and the point is not geography but dependence. Kings, allies, armies and clever negotiation cannot lift a person up or a people out of trouble. Only God can, because only God judges.

He also meant to steady people who were waiting. The words in verse 2, 'When I choose a time,' are spoken by God to people who have been asking 'How long?' They do not answer the question about the date, but they tell the community that the date exists and is fixed by a fair judge. The singer's response in verse 1 is to give thanks before the judgment arrives, since God's name is already 'near.'

Finally, the author wanted to warn any Israelite tempted to copy the arrogance of the nations. The commands of verses 4 and 5 are addressed to the proud and the wicked, but a congregation that sings them also hears them. The song is a promise to the humble and a mirror for the strong. A leader who sings it cannot go on boasting.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes God's way of governing, and the speaker is God himself, so its statements about judgment are declarations rather than advice. What it prescribes is a stance. Give thanks, verse 1. Do not boast, verses 4 and 5. Proclaim God and sing his praise, verse 9. Those are the commands that the reader can act on.

It would be a mistake to turn the psalm into a rule for reading every rise and fall in life. Verse 7 says God brings down one and exalts another, but it does not say that every rich person is wicked or that every poor person is righteous. Job, Psalm 73 and Ecclesiastes all know that in the present age the proud sometimes prosper. Verse 2 keeps the balance: the judgment comes 'when I choose a time,' which may be later than the sufferer would like.

Nor does verse 10, 'all the horns of the wicked I will cut off,' authorise believers to cut anything off. It is God's promise about God's action. The right response is the one Paul describes: 'leave room for God's wrath,' Romans 12:19, and meanwhile 'humble yourselves under God's mighty hand,' 1 Peter 5:6.

debates.question: Does the cup of verse 8 point to one particular judgment or to God's judgment on the wicked in every age?

views.label: A specific historical judgment
views.case: The psalm sits in a collection about enemies of Zion and its heading recalls a plea for survival. Read alongside Psalm 76, the cup could describe what happened to a specific hostile army, and the verbs are concrete, pouring and drinking.

views.label: A general and repeated principle
views.case: 'All the wicked of the earth' in verse 8 is universal, and the picture recurs in Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15-16 and Revelation 14:10 to describe God's judgment across history and at its end.

debates.bearing: Both agree that the cup is God's to pour. The psalm is not given a date by the debate, and the principle it states, that God alone gives and takes exaltation, applies whichever view is taken.

debates.question: Who speaks in verses 2 to 5 and in verse 10?

views.label: God speaks directly, through a prophetic voice in the worship
views.case: The pronouns are divine: 'I will judge,' 'I bear up its pillars,' 'I will cut off.' Asaph and his sons are described as prophesying with music, 1 Chronicles 25:1-2, so an oracle from God inside a psalm would be expected.

views.label: The king or a leader speaks for God
views.case: Some read verses 2 and 3 as the voice of Israel's king or a representative claiming to judge fairly, and treat the horns of verse 10 as royal language, as in Psalm 132:17.

debates.bearing: The difference does not touch the theology, because verse 7 makes clear that the judge is God. On the prophetic reading the psalm becomes a direct promise; on the royal reading the king's authority is borrowed from the same God.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is 'time' in verse 2. The Hebrew is the same as the 'meeting place' of Psalm 74:4 and 74:8, a word that means an appointed time or place. It is the word for the appointed feasts in Leviticus 23. In Psalm 74 the enemy destroyed the appointments; in Psalm 75 God declares that he keeps the one appointment that counts, the time of judgment. The translation 'When I choose' catches the sense that God takes the time in his own hand.

The second is 'fairly' in the same verse. The Hebrew word carries the sense of level ground or evenness, and it is the word used in Psalm 9:8, 'He governs the people with equity,' and Psalm 98:9, 'the peoples with equity.' The picture is of a judge whose scales are even. That is important for the reader who fears that the delay in verse 2 means the judge is careless: the timing is God's, and the justice is level.

The third is the noun for 'horn.' Verse 4 has the proud lift up their horn, verse 5 repeats it, and verse 10 has God cut off the horns of the wicked and lift the horns of the righteous. The horn was the weapon of the wild ox, as in Psalm 92:10, and by extension a symbol of strength, dignity and dynasty. The Bible can speak of a 'horn of salvation,' Psalm 18:2 and Luke 1:69, and also of the horns of hostile nations, as in Zechariah 1:18-21, where four horns that scattered Judah are met by four craftsmen who terrify them. So the horn is neutral until one asks whose it is and who lifted it.

The fourth is the word for 'cup', kos. In this psalm it is 'full of foaming wine mixed with spices' and poured 'to the dregs.' The 'foaming' and the 'mixed' signal a strong drink, and the 'dregs' are the sediment at the bottom that a drinker would normally avoid. Isaiah 51:17 uses the same picture for what Jerusalem drained. The kos can also be blessing, as in Psalm 16:5 and 23:5, and the same word is used in all these places. What decides the sense is who is drinking and what is in it.

The footnote to verse 9, 'Or proclaim it,' notes that the Hebrew can mean 'I will declare it forever' or 'I will proclaim Him forever'; either way, the singer's task is to tell what he has heard.

typology.type: The cup of foaming wine, verse 8
typology.fulfillment: The cup of judgment in Jeremiah 25:15-16 and Isaiah 51:17 is the pattern behind Jesus' words in Gethsemane, 'let this cup pass from Me,' Matthew 26:39, and 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' John 18:11. Christ drinks what verse 8 says the wicked must drink, and the escalation is that he drinks it in their place, so that God can say, as in Isaiah 51:22, 'you will never drink again.' The type falls short in that the psalm's cup is for those who resist; Christ's drinking of it opens the possibility of another cup, the new covenant in his blood, Luke 22:20. Those who refuse him are still warned of the cup, Revelation 14:10.

The horn of the righteous, lifted by God, becomes in Zechariah's song 'a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69, and Psalm 132:17 promised that God would make a horn grow for David. The correspondence is between God's promise to raise a strong one from David's line and the coming of Jesus. The escalation is that the horn is not just a strong king but a saviour who lifts his people with him. The type falls short in that earlier kings could be thrown down, as Psalm 89 laments; this horn cannot.

typology.type: Bringing down the proud and exalting the humble, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: Hannah, Mary and Jesus himself repeat the pattern, 1 Samuel 2:7-8, Luke 1:52 and Luke 18:14. In Philippians 2:6-11, the one who did not hold on to equality with God humbled himself to death on a cross, and 'therefore God exalted Him.' Christ is the pattern of the psalm's rule: he goes down and God raises him up. The type falls short in that for ordinary people humility is a discipline in a sinful heart, while Christ's humbling was voluntary and sinless.

typology.type: The pillars of the earth held steady, verse 3
typology.fulfillment: When the earth 'quakes,' God bears up its pillars. In Colossians 1:17 Christ is the one in whom 'all things hold together,' and Hebrews 1:3 says he sustains all things by his powerful word. The correspondence is that the stability of creation in a shaking world is a divine work. The escalation is that the Son is named as the one who holds it. The type falls short as a figure of the physical world, since the New Testament also looks to a future shaking after which what cannot be shaken remains, Hebrews 12:26-28.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ by the cup. Verse 8 shows a cup in the LORD's hand, full and strong, which the wicked drink to the last drop. When Jesus prays in Gethsemane, 'Father, if You are willing, take this cup from Me. Yet not My will, but Yours be done,' Luke 22:42, the cup He fears is this one. The image is not vague. Isaiah had heard God tell Jerusalem that He would take the cup of staggering from her hand and put it into the hands of her tormentors, Isaiah 51:22-23. The gospel is that the Judge Himself takes it, and John records His resolve, 'Shall I not drink the cup the Father has given Me?' John 18:11.

It leads to Christ by the pattern of humbling and lifting up. The psalm says of God, 'He brings down one and exalts another.' In Jesus the pattern is not two persons but one story. The Son of God, Philippians 2 tells us, humbled himself to the point of death, and 'therefore God exalted Him to the highest place.' The horn of verse 10 belongs to Him: Zechariah says God has 'raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of His servant David,' Luke 1:69. What Israel could only hear in a promise, 'the horns of the righteous will be exalted,' has come in the person of the Righteous One.

It leads to Christ by the judge who is fair. Verse 2 says, 'I will judge fairly,' and the New Testament says that the Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son, so that He is the one who will hold the appointed time. Jesus tells the high priest that He will be seen 'sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven,' Matthew 26:64. The time God chooses is the day of the return of Christ.

It leads to Christ also by contrast. The proud lift their horns and stretch their necks against heaven, verse 5. Christ is the one who, being in the form of God, did not cling to equality. The psalm warns the arrogant, and in the Gospels the only ones who are turned away are the self-exalted who insist they do not need a physician. The tax collector who beat his breast went home justified, Luke 18:14.

The reading has a limit that should be kept in view. The psalm does not mention a Messiah, and verse 8 is not a hidden prediction of Gethsemane. The link is the shared image of the cup and the shared principle of God's rule, which the New Testament writers themselves use when they speak of Jesus' suffering and exaltation. The psalm gives the vocabulary; the Gospels give the person who bears it.
study.god:
The first thing the psalm shows about God is that He is near. The opening line says 'Your Name is near,' and the people's evidence is that they can tell of His 'wondrous works.' Right after a psalm that asked where God was, this one begins with confidence in His presence. Nearness here does not mean that trouble is absent; it means that the God who speaks is within reach of the singer's voice.

He is the judge who is fair, and the psalm leaves no doubt that He is also the one who sets the calendar. 'When I choose a time' means that patience is not weakness. The delay that the sufferer feels as neglect is, from God's side, a matter of appointment. In 2 Peter 3:9 the same patience is a mercy for those who would otherwise be judged, and the psalm allows the reader to see that mercy in the interval. God's timing does not betray His justice.

He is the one who holds the world together. In verse 3 the earth and its people 'quake', and God says, 'it is I who bear up its pillars.' At the very moment He talks about judgment He is also speaking about preservation. The shaking is not the collapse of the created order but something inside His control. That should quiet the fear that when the powers of the world rise and fall, everything comes apart.

He is the God who alone exalts. Verse 6 shuts every other door: not east, not west, not the desert. This is an exclusive claim, and it fits the Old Testament's insistence that the LORD has no rivals. It also explains why the song of Hannah and the Magnificat are so similar in shape. When power is taken from God's hand and put in a human one, the human falls; when it is received from God, it lasts.

He is holy, and His wrath is not random. The cup is mixed, full of spice and foam, carefully prepared, and every wicked person of the earth drinks it. Holiness appears here as moral order: the world is not indifferent to arrogance. Yet the same God will have a cup that is different in the end, and Isaiah 51:22 shows Him taking the cup from the hand of His people.

And He is worthy of song. The psalm ends with the singer's vow, 'I will proclaim Him forever,' verse 9, and the singer is not pretending everything has been fixed. He is trusting the God who holds the appointment.

In worship, the psalm teaches us to give thanks before the verdict is visible and to confess our own temptation to lift our horn. It gives the humble a place to stand and the proud a warning they can still heed.

crossReferences.note: The enemy roared in God's 'meeting place,' using the same word for appointment that appears in Psalm 75:2. Read together, the enemy's destruction of God's appointed places is answered by God's own appointment of the time of judgment.

Hannah's song shares the horn, the warning against boasting, the God who brings low and lifts up, and the foundations of the earth. Psalm 75 sounds like a congregation's version of her prayer, and it shows that this vision of God runs through Israel's worship from its beginning.

Jerusalem is told she has drunk 'the cup of His fury' to the dregs, and then that God has taken it from her hand and will put it in the hands of her tormentors. It gives the psalm's cup a story with both a drinking and an ending.

Jeremiah takes the cup of the wine of wrath to make the nations drink and stagger. It shows that the cup of Psalm 75:8 is a familiar prophetic image for God's judgment on the nations, not just a poetic flourish.
Mary sings that God has brought down rulers from their thrones but has exalted the humble. She is echoing the pattern of Psalm 75:7 as the reversal of the world begins in the birth of her son.
Zechariah says God has raised up a horn of salvation in the house of David. It is the answer to the exalted horn of verse 10, and it shows the horn becoming a person.
Jesus prays that the cup might pass yet submits to the Father's will. Set beside verse 8, it shows the Son entering the judgment that the psalm says the wicked must drink.
Those who worship the beast will drink the wine of God's anger, poured undiluted into the cup of His wrath. It shows the image of verse 8 carried to its end in the last judgment.

'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble,' quoting Proverbs 3:34. It is the New Testament summary of the moral lesson of verses 4 to 7, applied to the church, which is told to take the low place now and leave the lifting to God.
Believers are told to humble themselves under God's mighty hand so that 'in due time' He may exalt them. It is the pastoral form of the psalm's promise that God will act in the time He chooses.
The psalmist thanks God for exalting his horn like that of a wild ox. It shows what verse 10 means in a positive sense, and how a believer can say that the strength he now has is a gift.

Moses pleads, 'do not destroy Your people, Your inheritance.' The psalm's tune title, Do Not Destroy, evokes the same prayer, placing the song in the line of intercession for a people who cannot save themselves.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story opens with a wonderful and dangerous gift. Human beings were made to rule under God, but the first temptation was to grasp at more, 'you will be like God,' Genesis 3:5. The picture of the lifted horn and the outstretched neck in Psalm 75 is that same grasp seen in kings and empires. Every tower that reached for heaven, Genesis 11:4, and every ruler who said 'I will ascend' in Isaiah 14:13, is an early form of what this psalm addresses.

Against that, the story shows a God who takes the low and lifts them. He chose a barren woman and her son, a slave people, a shepherd boy and a small tribe. Hannah's song expresses the pattern before the monarchy begins, 1 Samuel 2:8. The psalm says this is not chance but principle: 'exaltation comes neither from east nor west,' but from God. Israel's history, with its rises and falls, is the demonstration.

The psalm's position beside Psalm 74 matters for the story as well. When the temple was burned and the people carried away, it looked as if the proud had won. The exile is the time in which the Bible's most searching questions about God's justice are asked, and this psalm is one of the answers: the time is appointed, the cup is poured, the horns will be cut off. Prophets like Jeremiah and Isaiah gave the cup its long history, Jeremiah 25:15-16 and Isaiah 51:17, showing that even Israel had to drink from it.

The story turns in Jesus. He is the humble one whom God exalts, and He is the one who takes the cup. Mary's song at the very start of the Gospel picks up the psalm, Luke 1:52, and Zechariah's horn of salvation carries the promise forward, Luke 1:69. At the cross the proud powers are shown up and the humble one is raised, and the church is told to share His path of humility in the present, 1 Peter 5:6.

It ends in the new creation. Revelation 14:10 and 16:19 show the cup of wrath given to those who exalted themselves against God and His people, and Revelation 21:4 tells of a world where the humble are lifted for good and 'the former things have passed away.' The pillars that God bore up in verse 3 will stand in a world where nobody lifts a horn against heaven, and the song of the psalmist, 'I will proclaim Him forever,' becomes the song of every creature.

quiz.q: What does the congregation give thanks for in verse 1?

options.text: That God's Name is near and His wondrous works are declared among the people.
options.note: The psalm opens with thanksgiving rooted in God's nearness and known deeds.

options.text: A recent military victory described in detail.
options.note: No specific battle is described; the thanksgiving centers on God's nearness and works generally.

options.text: A new king's coronation ceremony.
options.note: No coronation is mentioned; the focus is thanksgiving for God's own nearness.

options.text: The rebuilding of a destroyed city.
options.note: No such rebuilding is described in this psalm.

quiz.q: What warning does God give to the proud and wicked, verses 4-5?

options.text: Not to boast or lift up their horn against heaven.
options.note: This is God's direct warning against arrogant self-exaltation.

options.text: To increase their wealth as quickly as possible.
options.note: The opposite; the warning is against boastful pride, not a call to gain wealth.

options.text: To build higher walls for protection.
options.note: No such instruction appears; the warning concerns pride, not fortifications.

options.text: To seek alliances with foreign nations.
options.note: The psalm addresses pride before God, not foreign policy.

quiz.q: According to verses 6-7, where does exaltation come from?

options.text: Neither from east, west, nor the desert, but from God alone, who judges.
options.note: This directly states that no direction or human source grants true exaltation, only God.

options.text: From military conquest alone.
options.note: The text explicitly denies that any earthly direction or power source grants exaltation.

options.text: From inherited royal bloodlines only.
options.note: The psalm attributes exaltation to God's judgment, not merely bloodline.

options.text: From the size of one's army.
options.note: The text denies any human source as the origin of true exaltation.

quiz.q: What does the cup in God's hand represent, verse 8?

options.text: Judgment that the wicked of the earth must drink down to the dregs.
options.note: This vivid image pictures inescapable divine judgment on the wicked.

options.text: A reward given only to the faithful.
options.note: The cup here specifically represents judgment on the wicked, not reward for the faithful.

options.text: A covenant meal shared among all nations.
options.note: The image is one of judgment poured out, not a shared covenant meal.

options.text: A blessing of abundant wine for a festival.
options.note: The context makes clear this cup is judgment, not festival blessing.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's theme connect most directly to the New Testament?

options.text: Mary's Magnificat echoes it directly, declaring God brings down rulers and lifts up the humble, Luke 1:52.
options.note: This is a clear and direct New Testament echo of the psalm's central theme.

options.text: It predicts the exact date of a future battle.
options.note: The psalm makes no such specific prediction.

options.text: It has no clear connection to the New Testament.
options.note: Its theme is directly echoed in Luke 1:52 and its cup imagery in Matthew 26:39.

options.text: It teaches that all wealth is inherently evil.
options.note: The psalm addresses pride and God's sovereign judgment, not wealth itself as inherently evil.

questions: The psalm opens with thanksgiving because God's Name is near, verse 1. What specific evidence of God's nearness can you give thanks for today?
God warns the proud not to lift up their horn or boast, verses 4-5. Where in your own life are you tempted toward that same self-exalting boastfulness?
The psalm insists that exaltation comes from God alone, not from any human direction or effort, verses 6-7. Where are you tempted to seek promotion or significance apart from God?
Jesus drank the very cup of judgment pictured in verse 8 so that His people would not have to. How does remembering what that cup cost Him change the way you receive God's mercy today?

The psalmist resolves to keep proclaiming God forever regardless of present circumstances, verse 9. What would it look like for you to keep praising God even while waiting for Him to set something right?

translationNotes.note: 'Do Not Destroy' is the name of a tune to which this psalm was set, shared with Psalms 57, 58, and 59, likely referencing a specific occasion of deliverance from destruction.
'I will proclaim Him' can also be rendered 'I will proclaim it,' referring either to God Himself or to His works; either reading fits the psalm's call to ongoing, forever praise.
